<b>Биологические часы.</b> Главные часы: The body clock. The master clock is the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus — ≈ 20,000 neurons with a ~24 h rhythm. Light on special retinal cells (melanopsin) sets it. In the evening darkness it lets the pineal gland release melatonin, the body’s “night” signal; cortisol peaks in the morning, temperature toward evening.
<b>Яркий экран вечером.</b> Синий свет э: A bright screen in the evening. Blue light from screens and lamps acts on the same retinal cells as daylight: the clock thinks it is still day, and melatonin release is suppressed and delayed. Falling asleep gets harder and waking up heavier. Night shifts and flights across time zones (jet lag) upset the clock the same way.
<b>Бодрствование.</b> Глаза открыты, на: Wake. Eyes open; the EEG shows fast low waves (beta, alpha with eyes closed). During the day adenosine builds up in the brain — “sleep pressure”; caffeine blocks its receptors, which is why it keeps you alert. Brief awakenings at night are normal and usually forgotten by morning.
<b>N1 — дремота</b> (несколько минут). М: N1 — drowsiness (a few minutes). Muscles relax, jerks may occur, eyes drift slowly. On the EEG the alpha rhythm gives way to theta waves. Easy to wake; people often feel they were not asleep.
<b>N2 — лёгкий сон</b>, около половины н: N2 — light sleep, about half the night. The EEG shows sleep spindles and K-complexes: the thalamus “disconnects” the cortex from outside sounds. Spindles are linked to consolidating skills learned during the day. Pulse and temperature drop.
<b>N3 — глубокий (медленный) сон</b> — в: N3 — deep (slow-wave) sleep — mostly in the first half of the night. Slow, tall delta waves; hard to wake. Growth hormone is released, and the glymphatic system flushes cerebrospinal fluid through the brain more actively, clearing waste including beta-amyloid.
<b>REM — быстрый сон</b> (сон с быстрыми: REM sleep (rapid eye movement), longer and longer toward morning. The EEG looks like wakefulness and the eyes move quickly, but the body muscles are paralyzed — so we do not act out our dreams. The most vivid dreams happen in REM; it matters for memory and emotions.
Треть жизни мы спим — и это не отдых моз: We spend a third of our lives asleep — and it is not rest for the brain but work: it sorts memories and washes out waste. When to sleep is decided by a clock in the hypothalamus that is set by light.
\n <div><h2>Циркадный ритм</h2>\n:
Circadian rhythm

Almost every cell has its own molecular clock (genes CLOCK, BMAL1, PER, CRY — a feedback loop of about 24 h). The suprachiasmatic nucleus synchronizes them by light: retina → retinohypothalamic tract → SCN → (via the spinal cord and the superior cervical ganglion) → pineal gland. Melatonin rises with darkness and peaks around 2–4 a.m.

How much sleep

Adults need 7–9 h, teenagers 8–10, newborns 14–17. Teenagers’ clocks naturally run later. A sleep cycle is ≈ 90 min; a night has 4–6 cycles: deep sleep early, REM toward morning.

Disorders

  • Insomnia; sleep apnea (pauses in breathing, snoring); narcolepsy (lack of orexin — sudden sleep attacks).
  • Sleep loss impairs attention and memory, increases appetite and the risk of diabetes, obesity and heart disease.
  • Helpful: a steady schedule, morning light, a dark cool bedroom, fewer screens and less caffeine in the evening.

Conventions

  • The head and brain are simplified; the path from the SCN to the pineal gland (via the spinal cord and the superior cervical ganglion) is drawn schematically.
  • Melatonin, cortisol and temperature curves are typical shapes in arbitrary units; the hypnogram is one adult night as an example.
  • Day and night are sped up; eye movements and brain “flushing” are illustrative, not to scale.
